title: Latest sign-in and app per user from a sign-in log export with LET, MAXIFS and XLOOKUP
summary: One spilled formula that reduces a long sign-in log table to a single row per user showing the most recent sign-in time and the app used.
body:
## What it does
A sign-in export from Microsoft Entra ID usually has thousands of rows per user. This formula returns one row per user with the latest sign-in timestamp and the application used at that moment, sorted so the most recent activity is on top. It spills, so there is nothing to fill down.

## Sample data layout
Excel table named SignIns (Insert > Table), headers in row 1:

| UserPrincipalName | SignInTime | App | Status |
| anna@contoso.example | 2026-11-18 08:12 | Microsoft Teams | Success |
| anna@contoso.example | 2026-11-19 17:40 | Outlook | Success |
| ben@contoso.example | 2026-11-12 09:05 | SharePoint Online | Failure |

SignInTime must be a real Excel date-time (not text). If the CSV imported it as text, convert it with Data > Text to Columns or with Power Query.

## The formula
Enter in one empty cell with free space below and to the right:

```
=LET(
  upn,  UNIQUE(SignIns[UserPrincipalName]),
  last, MAXIFS(SignIns[SignInTime], SignIns[UserPrincipalName], upn),
  app,  XLOOKUP(
          upn & "|" & last,
          SignIns[UserPrincipalName] & "|" & SignIns[SignInTime],
          SignIns[App],
          "n/a"),
  VSTACK(
    {"User","Last sign-in","App"},
    SORT(HSTACK(upn, last, app), 2, -1)
  )
)
```

Step by step: UNIQUE builds the user list. MAXIFS accepts an array as criteria, so it returns the maximum timestamp for every user at once. XLOOKUP then finds the row where the combined key "user|timestamp" matches, because a plain lookup on the user alone would return the first row, not the latest. HSTACK joins the three columns, SORT orders by column 2 descending, and VSTACK adds a header row.

## How to adapt
- Only successful sign-ins: add a criteria pair to MAXIFS, for example , SignIns[Status], "Success", and filter the lookup key the same way.
- Show the IP or location instead of the app: change the third argument of XLOOKUP to SignIns[IPAddress].
- Format the second column as date-time (yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm). Spilled results inherit formatting only from the first cell, so format the whole spill column.
- To keep only users who have not signed in for 30 days, wrap the SORT part in FILTER: FILTER(HSTACK(upn,last,app), last < TODAY()-30, "Nobody").

## Required permissions
None in Excel itself. To get the export you need a role that can read sign-in logs in Microsoft Entra ID, such as Reports Reader, Security Reader or Global Reader. Excel needs Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021 or later for LET, VSTACK and HSTACK; VSTACK and HSTACK need a current Microsoft 365 build.

## Common mistakes
- Using XLOOKUP on the user only: it returns the oldest row for each user.
- Timestamps stored as text: MAXIFS ignores text and returns 0.
- Floating point keys: the combined key converts the date to text with 15 significant digits on both sides, so it matches. If you round the timestamp in one place but not the other, the lookup returns n/a. Round both or neither.
- Blocking the spill range: any value in the cells below causes a #SPILL! error.

## Performance and scaling notes
The lookup compares a concatenated array against every row for each user, so cost grows with users times rows. Up to roughly 50,000 rows it recalculates instantly. For larger logs, aggregate in Power Query first (Group By with a Max operation) or add a helper column in the table that holds the key, and look that column up instead of building the array inside the formula.

title: Summarize accounts by email domain with TEXTAFTER, UNIQUE, COUNTIFS and SORTBY
summary: A spilled summary table that counts users per email domain, how many are enabled, and the enabled share, sorted by size, built from a user export.
body:
## What it does
Use it to spot guest-heavy domains, leftover domains after a merger, or domains with many disabled accounts. It reads a user export, extracts the domain of every address, and returns one row per domain with total accounts, enabled accounts and the enabled percentage.

## Sample data layout
Table named Users:

| DisplayName | UserPrincipalName | AccountEnabled |
| Anna Meyer | anna@contoso.example | TRUE |
| Ben Ortiz | ben@fabrikam.example | FALSE |
| Cho Lee | cho@fabrikam.example | TRUE |

AccountEnabled should be true boolean values. If the export contains the text True/False, convert the column in Power Query (Transform > Data Type > True/False) so the criteria below match.

## The formula
```
=LET(
  dom,   UNIQUE(TEXTAFTER(Users[UserPrincipalName], "@", -1)),
  total, COUNTIF(Users[UserPrincipalName], "*@" & dom),
  act,   COUNTIFS(Users[UserPrincipalName], "*@" & dom, Users[AccountEnabled], TRUE),
  VSTACK(
    {"Domain","Accounts","Enabled","Enabled %"},
    SORTBY(HSTACK(dom, total, act, ROUND(act/total, 3)), total, -1)
  )
)
```

TEXTAFTER with instance -1 takes the text after the last @, which is correct even for guest UPNs such as john_fabrikam.example#EXT#@contoso.onmicrosoft.com (the result is the tenant domain, so guests group under contoso.onmicrosoft.com). COUNTIF and COUNTIFS require a range in the first argument, which is why the table column is referenced directly and the domain list is turned into wildcard criteria. The wildcard *@domain matches only addresses that end with exactly @domain, so a.b@dev.contoso.example does not count for contoso.example.

## How to adapt
- Separate guests from members: add a column UserType and add Users[UserType], "Member" to COUNTIFS.
- Top five only: wrap the SORTBY in TAKE(..., 5).
- Show the share of all accounts instead: add ROUND(total/SUM(total),3) as another HSTACK column.
- Use the Mail column instead of UserPrincipalName if your UPN domain differs from the mail domain.

## Required permissions
None in Excel. The user export needs a role that can read users, for example Directory Readers, or the Graph permission User.Read.All if you export through Microsoft Graph or PowerShell. TEXTAFTER, VSTACK, HSTACK and TAKE need a current Microsoft 365 build of Excel.

## Common mistakes
- Passing a calculated array as the range argument of COUNTIF: this returns #VALUE!. Reference the table column and build the criteria array instead.
- Booleans stored as text: COUNTIFS with TRUE then returns 0. Check with =ISLOGICAL(Users[@AccountEnabled]).
- Trailing spaces in exported addresses: wrap the source in TRIM or clean the column in Power Query.

## Performance and scaling notes
COUNTIF with wildcards scans the whole column per domain. With 100,000 users and 200 domains this is still a fraction of a second. If the domain list is very long, add a Domain helper column to the table with =TEXTAFTER([@UserPrincipalName],"@",-1) and count on that column without wildcards, which is faster and easier to audit.

title: Find accounts missing from the HR list with FILTER and XMATCH, and the reverse check
summary: Reconcile an Entra user export against an HR roster in both directions to find orphaned accounts and employees without an account.
body:
## What it does
Joiner-mover-leaver checks usually start as a comparison of two lists. This pair of formulas returns (1) accounts that exist in the directory but not in HR, which are candidates for review or removal, and (2) HR employees who have no matching account yet. Matching is case-insensitive and ignores stray spaces.

## Sample data layout
Table Entra (from a directory export):

| DisplayName | Mail | Department |
| Anna Meyer | anna.meyer@contoso.example | Sales |

Table HR (from the HR system):

| Employee | WorkEmail | Status |
| Anna Meyer | Anna.Meyer@contoso.example | Active |

## Formula 1: accounts without an HR record
```
=LET(
  hrMail, TRIM(HR[WorkEmail]),
  hit,    ISNA(XMATCH(TRIM(Entra[Mail]), hrMail)),
  res,    FILTER(Entra, hit, "No orphaned accounts"),
  res
)
```

## Formula 2: HR employees without an account
```
=LET(
  dirMail, TRIM(Entra[Mail]),
  hit,     ISNA(XMATCH(TRIM(HR[WorkEmail]), dirMail)),
  FILTER(HR, hit * (HR[Status]="Active"), "Everyone has an account")
)
```

Place the two formulas on separate sheets, or far enough apart that their spill ranges do not collide. Add a counter cell above each: =IF(ISTEXT(A3), 0, ROWS(A3#)), where A3 is the formula cell. When the formula returns the fallback text, a plain ROWS would report 1, so the ISTEXT test is needed.

## How to adapt
- Match on employee ID instead of mail: replace both mail columns with the ID columns, and ensure both are the same data type (number versus text).
- Ignore service and shared mailbox accounts: add * (Entra[Department]<>"Service") to the first FILTER condition.
- Only enabled accounts: export AccountEnabled and multiply by (Entra[AccountEnabled]=TRUE).
- Fuzzy differences like alias addresses: match against a ProxyAddresses column using ISNUMBER(SEARCH(...)) in a MAP over the HR list, accepting the slower calculation.

## Required permissions
None in Excel. The directory export needs a role such as Directory Readers or User Administrator, or the Graph permission User.Read.All. Handle the HR file according to your data protection rules; do not store it in a widely shared library.

## Common mistakes
- Hidden characters: non-breaking spaces (CHAR(160)) are not removed by TRIM. Use SUBSTITUTE(x, CHAR(160), " ") inside TRIM if the export comes from a web page.
- Different mail domains between systems: normalise to the part before the @ with TEXTBEFORE if the domains legitimately differ.
- Treating the result as a deletion list: review each row, as contractors, rooms and break-glass accounts rarely appear in HR.

## Performance and scaling notes
XMATCH uses a binary-friendly linear search per item and is fast for tens of thousands of rows. If recalculation becomes slow, sort the lookup column and pass search_mode 2 (binary ascending) as the fourth argument of XMATCH, only when the list is genuinely sorted.

title: Stale account report with a threshold cell, FILTER and TODAY, including never-signed-in users
summary: A spilled report of enabled accounts whose last sign-in is older than a configurable number of days, with never-signed-in accounts labelled clearly.
body:
## What it does
Lists enabled accounts that have not signed in for N days, oldest first, and marks accounts that have never signed in. The number of days is a named cell, so non-technical colleagues can change it and watch the list update.

## Sample data layout
Table Users, plus a single cell named DaysInactive (Formulas > Name Manager, for example refers to Settings!$B$1 with value 90):

| DisplayName | UserPrincipalName | AccountEnabled | LastSignIn |
| Anna Meyer | anna@contoso.example | TRUE | 2026-11-18 |
| Old Service | oldsvc@contoso.example | TRUE | 2025-12-02 |
| New Hire | newhire@contoso.example | TRUE | (blank) |

LastSignIn comes from the signInActivity property when exporting through Microsoft Graph (lastSignInDateTime), or from the sign-in report. A blank cell means there is no recorded sign-in.

## The formula
```
=LET(
  cutoff, TODAY() - DaysInactive,
  stale,  (Users[AccountEnabled] = TRUE) * (Users[LastSignIn] < cutoff),
  since,  IF(Users[LastSignIn] = 0, "Never", TODAY() - INT(Users[LastSignIn])),
  data,   FILTER(HSTACK(Users[DisplayName], Users[UserPrincipalName], Users[LastSignIn], since), stale, "No stale accounts"),
  IF(ISTEXT(data), data,
     VSTACK({"Name","UPN","Last sign-in","Days inactive"}, SORT(data, 3, 1)))
)
```

A blank LastSignIn is treated as 0, which is always smaller than the cutoff, so never-signed-in accounts are included automatically and show "Never" in the last column. SORT on column 3 ascending puts blanks and the oldest dates first. The ISTEXT test prevents VSTACK from combining a header with the fallback message.

## How to adapt
- Exclude newly created accounts: add a CreatedDate column and multiply by (Users[CreatedDate] < cutoff), so someone hired yesterday is not flagged as never signed in.
- Exclude guests or service accounts with another multiplied condition on UserType or Department.
- Count only: =IF(ISTEXT(A3), 0, ROWS(A3#)) where A3 holds the formula.
- Highlight rows older than 180 days: apply conditional formatting to the spill using =$D3>180, taking care that "Never" text compares as greater than any number in Excel; add ISNUMBER if you want it excluded.

## Required permissions
Excel needs none. For the data: reading signInActivity through Microsoft Graph requires the AuditLog.Read.All permission together with User.Read.All, and the tenant needs Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2. The interactive and non-interactive sign-in timestamps are different properties; decide which one your policy uses.

## Common mistakes
- Comparing text dates: if LastSignIn arrives as text such as 2026-11-18T08:12:00Z, the comparison is wrong. Convert in Power Query with DateTimeZone.FromText.
- Disabling accounts directly from the list: stale does not always mean unused, for example for yearly processes and shared mailboxes.
- Forgetting the time zone: UTC timestamps near midnight can shift the day count by one.

## Performance and scaling notes
All calculations are single pass over the table and TODAY() is the only volatile part. The workbook recalculates whenever it opens; if you use it as a monthly snapshot, replace TODAY() with a fixed report date cell to keep results reproducible.

title: Reusable LAMBDA helpers for UPN cleanup, domain extraction and guest detection
summary: Define CleanUPN, UpnDomain, IsGuest and GuestToMail once in Name Manager, then reuse them across sheets with MAP and BYROW.
body:
## What it does
Identity exports are messy: mixed case, trailing spaces, non-breaking spaces and guest UPNs of the form john_fabrikam.example#EXT#@contoso.onmicrosoft.com. Instead of repeating nested SUBSTITUTE and TRIM calls, define small named LAMBDA functions once and use them like built-in functions.

## Sample data layout
Table Users:

| UserPrincipalName |
| Anna.Meyer@contoso.example |
| john_fabrikam.example#EXT#@contoso.onmicrosoft.com |
|  ben@contoso.example  |

## Define the functions
Formulas > Name Manager > New. Scope: Workbook. Enter the name and paste the formula into Refers to.

Name CleanUPN:
```
=LAMBDA(x, LOWER(TRIM(SUBSTITUTE(x, CHAR(160), " "))))
```

Name UpnDomain:
```
=LAMBDA(upn, IFERROR(TEXTAFTER(CleanUPN(upn), "@", -1), ""))
```

Name IsGuest:
```
=LAMBDA(upn, ISNUMBER(SEARCH("#EXT#", upn)))
```

Name GuestToMail (recovers the original address, because the @ of the external address was replaced by the last underscore):
```
=LAMBDA(upn,
  LET(
    p, TEXTBEFORE(CleanUPN(upn), "#ext#"),
    n, LEN(p) - LEN(SUBSTITUTE(p, "_", "")),
    SUBSTITUTE(p, "_", "@", n)
  )
)
```

## Use them in the sheet
Normalised UPN for the whole column (spills):
```
=MAP(Users[UserPrincipalName], CleanUPN)
```

Member or guest label:
```
=MAP(Users[UserPrincipalName], LAMBDA(u, IF(IsGuest(u), "Guest", "Member")))
```

Original external address, only for guests:
```
=MAP(Users[UserPrincipalName], LAMBDA(u, IF(IsGuest(u), GuestToMail(u), CleanUPN(u))))
```

A one-line label per user built with BYROW:
```
=BYROW(Users[UserPrincipalName], LAMBDA(r, UpnDomain(r) & " / " & IF(IsGuest(r), "G", "M")))
```

## How to adapt
- Add helpers for your own naming convention, for example a function that builds the expected sAMAccountName from first and last name.
- To share across workbooks, keep the definitions in a template (.xltx) or in an add-in workbook.
- Name functions with a prefix such as fx so they do not clash with future built-in names.

## Required permissions
None. Named LAMBDA functions need Microsoft 365 Excel (Windows, Mac or web). Functions defined with Name Manager are stored in the workbook; there is no tenant setting to enable.

## Common mistakes
- Forgetting the leading equals sign in Refers to.
- Naming a function like a cell reference (for example UPN1) or like an existing function.
- Calling a LAMBDA with the wrong number of arguments gives #VALUE!. Check the parameter list.
- Assuming #EXT# is always upper case: SEARCH is case-insensitive, FIND is not. The helpers lower-case first for that reason.
- Recursion: LAMBDA can call itself by name, but there is a recursion limit; avoid it for lists with thousands of items.

## Performance and scaling notes
MAP calls the lambda once per element. For simple operations, a direct array formula such as LOWER(TRIM(range)) is faster; reserve MAP for logic that cannot be vectorised, like the IF in the guest conversion. Function calls nest cheaply, but deeply layered LAMBDAs in large tables make debugging harder, so test each helper on three sample rows first.

title: Cloud cost by department: top five ranking and a month-by-month matrix with SUMIFS and TAKE
summary: Turn a cost export with a department tag into a ranked top-five table and a department by month matrix using spilled arrays.
body:
## What it does
Cost exports from Azure Cost Management or a license reconciliation list tens of thousands of line items. These two formulas aggregate them without a PivotTable: a ranked top five of departments and a full department-by-month matrix that updates when the table grows.

## Sample data layout
Table named Costs (an export where a department tag has been added):

| Date | ResourceGroup | Department | CostUSD |
| 2026-09-03 | rg-web-prod | Marketing | 41.20 |
| 2026-09-03 | rg-data | Finance | 118.75 |
| 2026-10-01 | rg-web-prod | Marketing | 39.90 |

Date must be a true date. Rows with an empty Department end up in the blank group, so fill them with "Untagged" in Power Query first; it makes the gap in your tagging visible.

## Formula 1: top five departments with share of total
```
=LET(
  d,     UNIQUE(Costs[Department]),
  cost,  SUMIFS(Costs[CostUSD], Costs[Department], d),
  share, cost / SUM(cost),
  VSTACK({"Department","Cost USD","Share"},
         TAKE(SORTBY(HSTACK(d, cost, share), cost, -1), 5))
)
```

## Formula 2: department by month matrix
```
=LET(
  d,     SORT(UNIQUE(Costs[Department])),
  mEnd,  TRANSPOSE(SORT(UNIQUE(DATE(YEAR(Costs[Date]), MONTH(Costs[Date]) + 1, 0)))),
  mPrev, DATE(YEAR(mEnd), MONTH(mEnd), 0),
  body,  SUMIFS(Costs[CostUSD], Costs[Department], d,
                Costs[Date], ">" & mPrev, Costs[Date], "<=" & mEnd),
  VSTACK(HSTACK("Department", mEnd), HSTACK(d, body))
)
```

DATE(year, month+1, 0) returns the last day of the month and works on arrays, which avoids the limitation that EOMONTH does not accept ranges directly. SUMIFS with a column of departments and a row of month boundaries returns a two-dimensional result, so the matrix is produced by a single call. Format the header row as mmm yyyy and the body as currency.

## How to adapt
- Add a total column: wrap with HSTACK(body, BYROW(body, LAMBDA(r, SUM(r)))).
- Rank by growth: subtract the second to last column of body from the last one (INDEX(body,,COLUMNS(body)) minus INDEX(body,,COLUMNS(body)-1)) and sort by the difference.
- Another dimension: replace Department with SubscriptionName, ResourceGroup or a tag column.
- Only one year: add Costs[Date], ">="&DATE(2026,1,1) to the SUMIFS pairs and filter the month list accordingly.

## Required permissions
None in Excel. To export costs you need Cost Management Reader (or higher) on the subscription or billing scope, plus the export or download permission of your portal. Do not paste billing account identifiers into shared workbooks.

## Common mistakes
- Dates stored as text: SUMIFS compares numbers and returns 0.
- Using EOMONTH on a range: it returns #VALUE!; use the DATE trick or add +0.
- Mixing currencies in one column: convert first.
- Leaving blank tags in: the blank group appears as an empty first row and distorts the ranking.

## Performance and scaling notes
SUMIFS over an Excel table is efficient up to hundreds of thousands of rows, but the matrix formula evaluates departments times months times rows. For very large exports, pre-aggregate by day and department in Power Query (Group By) and point the formulas at the smaller table.

title: Explode semicolon-separated group memberships into a long table with TEXTSPLIT and REDUCE
summary: Convert a column that lists groups per user into one row per user and group, then count members per group, using REDUCE, TEXTSPLIT and VSTACK.
body:
## What it does
Exports often contain one cell such as Sales-EU;Finance;All-Staff per user. That layout is impossible to count or filter. The formulas turn it into a tidy two-column list (user, group) and then summarise how many users each group has.

## Sample data layout
Table Users:

| UserPrincipalName | Groups |
| anna@contoso.example | Sales-EU;Finance;All-Staff |
| ben@contoso.example | All-Staff |
| cho@contoso.example | (blank) |

## Formula 1: long format
```
=LET(
  n, ROWS(Users),
  raw, DROP(
    REDUCE("", SEQUENCE(n),
      LAMBDA(acc, i,
        LET(
          g, TRIM(TOCOL(TEXTSPLIT(INDEX(Users[Groups], i) & "", ";"))),
          VSTACK(acc, HSTACK(IF(g = g, INDEX(Users[UserPrincipalName], i), ""), g))
        )
      )
    ), 1),
  FILTER(raw, INDEX(raw, , 2) <> "", "No memberships")
)
```

How it works: for every row index i, TEXTSPLIT cuts the cell at the semicolons, TOCOL turns the result into a column, and TRIM cleans each group name. IF(g = g, upn, "") repeats the user name for each group so the two columns have equal height. VSTACK appends the block to the accumulator, DROP removes the dummy first row, and FILTER removes blank group names (users without groups). Concatenating & "" turns an empty cell into an empty string so TEXTSPLIT does not receive a zero.

## Formula 2: members per group
Assuming Formula 1 is in cell F2 and spills:
```
=LET(
  grp, INDEX(F2#, , 2),
  g,   SORT(UNIQUE(grp)),
  n,   MAP(g, LAMBDA(x, SUM(--(grp = x)))),
  VSTACK({"Group","Members"}, SORTBY(HSTACK(g, n), n, -1))
)
```

## How to adapt
- Different delimiter: change ";" in TEXTSPLIT, or pass an array of delimiters such as {";",","}.
- Pivot instead of formulas: copy Formula 1 as values and insert a PivotTable counting Group by UserPrincipalName.
- Group names containing the delimiter must be quoted in the export; fix at source or use Power Query's Split Column by Delimiter with quote handling.

## Required permissions
None in Excel. The group lists come from an export; if you generate it with Microsoft Graph, the account needs GroupMember.Read.All or User.Read.All with Group.Read.All and a role such as Directory Readers. TEXTSPLIT, TOCOL, DROP and VSTACK need a current Microsoft 365 build.

## Common mistakes
- Forgetting to wrap TEXTSPLIT output in TOCOL: a row-shaped array would not stack correctly.
- Leading spaces after semicolons produce duplicate group names that look identical; TRIM prevents this.
- Referencing the spill range with a typed range instead of the # operator: new rows would be ignored.

## Performance and scaling notes
REDUCE with VSTACK copies the accumulator on every step, so runtime grows roughly with the square of the row count. It is comfortable for a few thousand users. For tens of thousands, use Power Query: select the Groups column, Split Column > By Delimiter > Advanced > Split into Rows, and load the result; it is faster and uses less memory.

title: Power Query M: combine a folder of CSV exports and keep the source file name
summary: A Power Query M script that appends all CSV files in a folder, tags each row with its file name, applies types and removes duplicates.
body:
## What it does
When an admin portal or script produces one CSV per day or per tenant, you want a single table that grows when you drop in a new file. This Power Query M script reads every CSV in a folder, promotes headers, keeps the file name as a column for traceability, converts types with an explicit culture, and removes duplicate rows.

## Sample data layout
Folder C:\Exports\SignIns contains files such as signins-2026-11-18.csv and signins-2026-11-19.csv. Each file has the columns:

| UserPrincipalName | CreatedDateTime | AppDisplayName | IPAddress | StatusCode |
| anna@contoso.example | 2026-11-19T08:12:00Z | Microsoft Teams | 203.0.113.10 | 0 |

## The M script
Data > Get Data > From Other Sources > Blank Query > Advanced Editor, paste:

```
let
  FolderPath = "C:\Exports\SignIns",
  Files   = Folder.Files(FolderPath),
  CsvOnly = Table.SelectRows(Files, each Text.Lower([Extension]) = ".csv" and not Text.StartsWith([Name], "~")),
  Parsed  = Table.AddColumn(CsvOnly, "Data", each
              Table.PromoteHeaders(
                Csv.Document([Content], [Delimiter = ",", Encoding = 65001, QuoteStyle = QuoteStyle.Csv]),
                [PromoteAllScalars = true])),
  Slim    = Table.SelectColumns(Parsed, {"Name", "Data"}),
  Cols    = List.Distinct(List.Combine(List.Transform(Slim[Data], each Table.ColumnNames(_)))),
  Expanded = Table.ExpandTableColumn(Slim, "Data", Cols, Cols),
  Renamed = Table.RenameColumns(Expanded, {{"Name", "SourceFile"}}),
  Typed   = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Renamed, {
              {"CreatedDateTime", type datetimezone},
              {"StatusCode", Int64.Type},
              {"UserPrincipalName", type text},
              {"AppDisplayName", type text},
              {"IPAddress", type text}}, "en-US"),
  Distinct = Table.Distinct(Typed, {"UserPrincipalName", "CreatedDateTime", "AppDisplayName"})
in
  Distinct
```

Explanation: Folder.Files lists all files recursively, including files in sub folders. The filter excludes temporary Office lock files that start with a tilde. Csv.Document with Encoding 65001 reads UTF-8. The list of column names is computed from all files, so a column added in a later export does not break the query. The culture argument in TransformColumnTypes avoids wrong date parsing on a machine with a different regional setting. Table.Distinct removes rows that appear in overlapping exports.

## How to adapt
- Use a parameter: Home > Manage Parameters > New, and replace the FolderPath line with the parameter name, so colleagues can point the query to their own folder.
- SharePoint folder instead of local: replace the first step with SharePoint.Files("https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Reports", [ApiVersion = 15]) and filter on [Folder Path].
- Semicolon-separated files: change the Delimiter to ";".
- Load as connection only and merge it with other queries for lookups.

## Required permissions
Read access to the folder. For SharePoint folders, the account used in Data > Data source settings needs at least Read permission on the library. No Microsoft Graph permission is involved.

## Common mistakes
- Hard-coded column list in ExpandTableColumn: fails when a file lacks a column. The dynamic list above avoids that.
- Different header casing between files creates two columns.
- Leaving type detection on automatic: the first file decides, and later files can produce errors in some rows.
- Opening the workbook on another PC where the folder path does not exist; use a parameter or a SharePoint location.

## Performance and scaling notes
Power Query reads each file once per refresh. Hundreds of files of a few MB each refresh in seconds to minutes. Filter files by name or date as early as possible (for example on [Date modified]) so older files are never parsed. Disable background data previews when authoring very large folders.

title: Power Query M: flatten a Microsoft Graph JSON export with nested signInActivity
summary: Load a saved Graph users JSON response into Excel, expand nested records and lists, and convert ISO timestamps into proper date-time values.
body:
## What it does
Responses from Microsoft Graph are JSON with nested objects such as signInActivity and lists such as businessPhones. This script loads a JSON file saved from Graph Explorer, a script or a tool, expands the nested parts into columns, and turns ISO 8601 text into real dates for filtering and charts.

## Sample data layout
A file users.json with the structure Graph returns:

```
{
  "value": [
    {
      "id": "[user-object-id]",
      "displayName": "Anna Meyer",
      "userPrincipalName": "anna@contoso.example",
      "accountEnabled": true,
      "businessPhones": ["+49 711 000000"],
      "signInActivity": {
        "lastSignInDateTime": "2026-11-18T08:12:00Z",
        "lastNonInteractiveSignInDateTime": "2026-11-19T02:00:00Z"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

## The M script
Data > Get Data > From Other Sources > Blank Query > Advanced Editor:

```
let
  FilePath = "C:\Exports\users.json",
  Raw      = Json.Document(File.Contents(FilePath)),
  Items    = Raw[value],
  AsTable  = Table.FromList(Items, Splitter.SplitByNothing(), {"Record"}, null, ExtraValues.Error),
  Expanded = Table.ExpandRecordColumn(AsTable, "Record",
               {"id", "displayName", "userPrincipalName", "accountEnabled", "businessPhones", "signInActivity"}),
  Phones   = Table.TransformColumns(Expanded, {{"businessPhones",
               each if _ = null or List.IsEmpty(_) then null else Text.Combine(List.Transform(_, Text.From), "; "), type text}}),
  Activity = Table.ExpandRecordColumn(Phones, "signInActivity",
               {"lastSignInDateTime", "lastNonInteractiveSignInDateTime"},
               {"LastSignIn", "LastNonInteractiveSignIn"}),
  Typed    = Table.TransformColumns(Activity, {
               {"LastSignIn", each if _ = null or _ = "" then null else DateTimeZone.FromText(_), type datetimezone},
               {"LastNonInteractiveSignIn", each if _ = null or _ = "" then null else DateTimeZone.FromText(_), type datetimezone},
               {"accountEnabled", each _, type logical}})
in
  Typed
```

Notes: ExpandRecordColumn takes the field names explicitly, so list only the properties you selected in the Graph query. The phone numbers are a JSON array and become a List value; the transformation joins them into one text cell. Users without sign-in data may have signInActivity set to null, and Table.ExpandRecordColumn handles null cells by returning nulls in the new columns. Graph returns 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z for accounts that never signed in; add a step that replaces dates earlier than 2000 with null if you prefer blanks.

## How to adapt
- Several pages: save each page and use Folder.Files plus the combine pattern, or store the pages as one array.
- Convert the time zone: DateTimeZone.SwitchZone(value, 1) for central European time, then DateTimeZone.RemoveZone to get a plain datetime.
- Different resources (groups, devices): change the field list in ExpandRecordColumn; the pattern is the same.
- Live data from Graph requires an authenticated connector; the Web connector with anonymous authentication cannot supply a token safely, so prefer a scheduled export (for example from PowerShell) written to SharePoint or a folder.

## Required permissions
Excel needs read access to the JSON file only. To produce the file, the Graph call needs User.Read.All, and AuditLog.Read.All for signInActivity, plus Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2.

## Common mistakes
- Pasting access tokens into M code to call Graph directly: tokens expire within an hour and are a security risk. Never store them in a workbook.
- Expanding a field that does not exist in every record without a default: the whole expansion fails. Use Record.FieldOrDefault inside a custom column for optional fields.
- Treating the timestamp as local time: the trailing Z means UTC.

## Performance and scaling notes
Json.Document loads the whole file in memory. Files of 50 to 100 MB are acceptable, larger ones should be split at the source or filtered with $select and $filter in the Graph request. Keep only the columns you need to reduce refresh time.

title: Forecast SharePoint storage growth with TREND and SEQUENCE and find the month a quota is exceeded
summary: Project the next twelve months of tenant or site storage use from monthly history and show the first month that exceeds the quota.
body:
## What it does
Admins often export storage used per month from the SharePoint admin center or from usage reports and need to know when the tenant or a site will hit its quota. These formulas fit a linear trend to the history, project the next twelve months, flag months over quota, and report the first month the quota is exceeded.

## Sample data layout
Table Storage with one row per month (first day of the month) and a named cell Quota holding the limit in GB:

| Month | UsedGB |
| 2026-01-01 | 812.4 |
| 2026-02-01 | 835.0 |
| 2026-03-01 | 861.9 |

Use at least six data points. Quota is a named cell, for example 1200.

## Formula 1: twelve-month forecast
```
=LET(
  h,  Storage[Month],
  y,  Storage[UsedGB],
  nd, DATE(YEAR(MAX(h)), MONTH(MAX(h)) + SEQUENCE(12), 1),
  fc, ROUND(TREND(y, h, nd), 1),
  VSTACK({"Month","Forecast GB","Over quota?"},
         HSTACK(nd, fc, IF(fc > Quota, "Yes", "No")))
)
```

DATE accepts the array produced by SEQUENCE, so the twelve future first-of-month dates are created in one step. TREND fits a straight line through the history and evaluates it at the new dates. Format the first column as mmm yyyy.

## Formula 2: first month over quota
```
=LET(
  h,  Storage[Month],
  y,  Storage[UsedGB],
  nd, DATE(YEAR(MAX(h)), MONTH(MAX(h)) + SEQUENCE(36), 1),
  fc, TREND(y, h, nd),
  XLOOKUP(TRUE, fc > Quota, nd, "Not within 36 months")
)
```

## Formula 3: average monthly growth
```
=ROUND(SLOPE(Storage[UsedGB], Storage[Month]) * 30.4375, 1)
```
The slope is GB per day, multiplied by the average days per month.

## How to adapt
- Exponential growth: replace TREND with GROWTH(y, h, nd) when growth is percentage-based, for example because of Copilot-driven content creation or migrations.
- Per site: add a Site column and wrap the logic in a LAMBDA that takes a site name and uses FILTER on the table; call it with MAP over UNIQUE(Storage[Site]).
- Plan a purchase threshold: compare against 90 percent of Quota to get a warning date.
- Chart: select the forecast spill and Insert > Line Chart; the chart follows the spill range when you reference it with the # operator.

## Required permissions
None in Excel. The history comes from SharePoint admin center usage data or reports; viewing it requires the SharePoint Administrator or Global Reader role, and Reports Reader for usage reports.

## Common mistakes
- Treating one-off migrations as trend: exclude outlier months or fit only the period after the migration.
- Using text months such as "Nov 2026": TREND needs real dates or numbers.
- Mixing GB and TB between months.
- Forgetting that recycle bin and version history count toward storage; a trend of content size alone underestimates consumption.

## Performance and scaling notes
These formulas operate on tens of rows and are instant. The main risk is not speed but model quality: a linear fit on twelve points is a rough guide. Re-check the forecast each month and keep the dated snapshots rather than overwriting history.
